newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Canada aims to boost wheat sales in Asia.
newsitem.headline: Canada aims to boost wheat sales in Asia.

text.p: Canada expects to boost its share of Asia's wheat market as consumers' incomes rise and they eat less rice, but it sees competition from the United States and Australia, a Canadian official said Thursday.
Gordon Machej, commissioner of the Canadian Wheat Board, also said Canada was doing commercial testing on a variety of wheat to be used specifically to make noodles.
"We are confident about business in the long term in Asia. As the population increases and has more money to spend, we will see an increase in demand," he told Reuters in an interview.
"We see more demand developing in South Korea, Thailand, Indonesia, Malaysia and the Philippines," he said. "We see opportunities to increase our market share."
Machej was in Indonesia as part of a delegation led by Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale to boost trade ties, especially in the agricultural sector.
Machej singled out the Indonesian market for its growth potential because of its 200 million population -- making it the world's fourth most populous country -- and growing affluence.
Industry sources said Indonesia imported some four million metric tons of wheat in 1996, up 10 percent from the previous year, to feed the rapid growth in the noodle industry.
Growing affluence has seen an increasing number of Indonesians reduce consumption of rice in favour of noodles.
Indonesia's PT Indofood Sukses Makmur -- part of the Salim Group controlled by ethnic Chinese tycoon Liem Sioe Liong -- is reputed to be one of the world's top noodle makers.

Machej said Canada's share of the Indonesian wheat market had risen to 30 percent in 1996 from a "low to mid-20 percent" while its share of the Thai market had increased to some 30 percent from about 20 percent.
"In January, we signed an agreement with Thai millers to supply 200,000 tons annually over five years," he said.
Machej said Canada's push to sell more wheat in Asia could face competition from the United States and Australia.

"Our main competition will come from the United States and Australia, and to some extent Argentina," he said. "Australia has some advantage in that they are close by and have a shorter sailing time. So we see them as a competitor."
He said Canada was growing a new variety of wheat to be used specifically for noodle production, adding that consumer testing was being carried out in countries such as Indonesia.
"Commercial shipments are expected after the 1997 harvest in August-September," he said. "If we have several hundred thousand tons this year, we'll be happy."
He said Canada was encouraging cultivation of the variety by assuring farmers delivery contracts for all of their output.
